summary.text: A geomagnetic reversal is a change in Earth's magnetic field in which magnetic north and magnetic south swap places.
Reversals appear to come at random, with at least 183 in the last 83 million years, the latest about 780,000 years ago.
New sea floor is magnetized in the field's direction as it forms, so spreading from a ridge leaves pairs of magnetic stripes, the first key test of seafloor spreading.

facts.label: Busiest stretch
facts.value: Five reversals in a million years, around 72 Ma

items.prompt: A geologist finds an old lava flow whose magnetism points the opposite way to today's field. What is the best explanation?

options.label: Lava always records the opposite of the field
The iron in old rock slowly turns itself around
Her compass was badly out of calibration
It cooled while Earth's field had the opposite polarity

items.explain: Most volcanic rocks keep a trace of the field as it was when they cooled, so a reversed rock cooled during a time of reversed polarity.

items.prompt: Over the last 83 million years, about how often has Earth's field flipped, on average?

options.label: About every 11 years
About every 4,500 years
About every 450,000 years
About every 45 million years

items.explain: At least 183 reversals in 83 million years works out to roughly one every 450,000 years.

items.prompt: New sea floor forms at a ridge and moves outward on both sides, while the field flips now and then. What pattern would a ship towing a magnetometer find?

options.label: Stripes running across the ridge at right angles
Paired stripes parallel to the ridge on each side
One magnetic direction over the whole ocean
Scattered patches with no pattern at all

items.explain: Rock is magnetized in the field's direction as it forms, so spreading from a central ridge produces pairs of stripes parallel to the ridge.

items.prompt: The field turns around for only a few hundred years and then goes back to how it was. What do scientists call this?

options.label: An excursion
A full reversal
A chron
A pole swap

items.explain: Short inversions lasting only a few hundred years, like the Laschamp event, are classed as excursions rather than full reversals.

items.prompt: Someone counts the years since the last flip to predict exactly when the next one is due. Why won't that work?

options.label: Flips follow a fixed clock that already ran out
Flips seem to come at random
Flips happen only after big asteroid impacts
Flips stopped millions of years ago

items.explain: Reversals appear statistically random, and their rate has varied widely over time, so no fixed gap can be counted on.

items.prompt: Rock layers on two different continents show the same sequence of magnetic flips. What can a geologist reasonably conclude?

options.label: The layers likely formed at matching times
The continents were once a single rock
The layers formed in the same place
One set of layers must be fake

items.explain: Because the magnetic field is global, similar patterns of magnetic change at different sites can be used to work out ages across locations.
